title: Nirvana Day again

cards: A doctor comes home from a long trip and finds his children rolling on the floor. While he was away, they drank poison. Some still have their wits, and take the medicine he mixes.
The others, their minds turned, won't touch it. So the doctor does something strange. He leaves again, and sends word home: your father is dead.
You met it in the Lotus Sutra this year; it returns on Nirvana Day, the day the Buddha's passing is remembered, because the Lotus tells it about that very passing.

teach.b: On day six ninety-two you met the scene the schools share: the Buddha lying down between two sal trees at Kusinara, and his last instruction, which in paraphrase says that everything put together comes apart, so keep going with care.
First, the Pali texts the Theravada keeps. A short book of sayings, the Itivuttaka, speaks of two elements of nibbana.
One is nibbana with something remaining: an awakened person still alive, still feeling pleasant and painful things, but with greed, hatred and delusion gone.
The other is nibbana with nothing remaining, when that life ends and all that was felt simply grows cool. The passing is real and complete: a fire gone out. Second, the Lotus Sutra.
In its chapter on the lifespan of the Tathagata, the Buddha says he awoke immeasurable ages ago, and that his passing is a skillful means. In plain sight forever, people would grow careless.
Like the doctor, he appears to go.
In their grief the children come to their senses and drink the medicine. Then, the story says, the father comes home.
Third, the Diamond Sutra, near its end: the Tathagata doesn't come from anywhere and doesn't go anywhere, and that, it says, is why he is called the Tathagata.
Each school explains its own reading, and this path doesn't rank them. Some hear one thing shared with those last words: each ending is put to work, to wake the ones still here.
Even where the Buddha never really left, the ending has to look real, or nobody takes the medicine.

how: In Japan and other East Asian communities, temples keep Nirvana Day with chanting, sutra reading and a painted scroll of the passing; in Theravada lands the passing is remembered on Vesak together with the birth and the awakening.

o: the day the Buddha's final passing is remembered
the day the Buddha first reached awakening
the day monks finish their rains retreat

games.q: one passing, three readings: tap the pairs.
p: a doctor who seems to leave

s: in the Lotus story, all the poisoned children take the medicine right away
some refuse it; only the news of their father's death brings them to their senses.
the Itivuttaka speaks of nibbana with something remaining and with nothing remaining
the first while an awakened person still lives; the second when that life ends.
this path names one school's reading of the passing as the right one
each school explains its own reading, and none is ranked.

games.q: you're the doctor. your children drank poison, and some refuse the medicine you made. what do you do?
o: leave, and send word that you have died.
wait at home until they change their minds.
games.why: in the Lotus Sutra he goes away and sends word of his death. in their grief they take the medicine, and then he comes home.

practice: Let three or four out-breaths finish completely. Then let one ending from this past year come to mind, a job, a home, a friend who moved away, and ask it the doctor's question: did this ending wake anything up?
Don't push for an answer; if sadness comes, let it sit beside you, and if grief ever feels like too much to carry alone, you can call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Nirvana Day. The day remembering the Buddha's final passing, his parinirvana, kept on different calendars and read in different ways by the schools. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali parinibbana (Sanskrit parinirvana): the final nirvana at an awakened one's death.

carryVoice: Your line: all things end. And some endings wake the ones still here. See you tomorrow, for Losar.
